```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

library(AlphaSimR)
```

`AlphaSimR` was written with plants and animals in mind, but nothing in
it requires an organism to be diploid for its whole life. This article
shows how to simulate the breeding of a fungus whose life cycle
alternates between haploid and diploid stages. It begins by matching
each stage of that life cycle to the functions that model it, then uses
them to simulate a published breeding program: the introgression of a
sporeless mutation into a commercial strain of oyster mushroom
(*Pleurotus ostreatus*). It ends with a list of what `AlphaSimR` can and
cannot represent, which should be read before modeling any other
species.

## Fungal life cycles in AlphaSimR

The edible mushrooms are basidiomycetes, and most of them share the same
basic life cycle. A spore germinates into a haploid mycelium called a
monokaryon, whose cells each carry one nucleus. When two compatible
monokaryons meet, their hyphae fuse but their nuclei do not: the result
is a dikaryon, a mycelium whose cells each carry one nucleus from each
parent. The dikaryon is the stage that is cultivated. It grows
vegetatively, it is what spawn producers propagate and sell, and it is
what forms mushrooms. Inside the gills of a mushroom, the two nuclei of
a cell finally fuse and the resulting diploid nucleus immediately
undergoes meiosis, producing four haploid spores that start the cycle
again.

Each of these steps has a counterpart in `AlphaSimR`.

| Stage                       | Biology                           | `AlphaSimR`                       |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Monokaryon                  | One haploid nucleus               | A `Pop` with `ploidy = 1`         |
| Mating                      | Two monokaryons fuse              | `mergeGenome()`                   |
| Dikaryon                    | Two nuclei, unfused               | A `Pop` with `ploidy = 2`         |
| Fruiting and sporulation    | Karyogamy, then meiosis           | `reduceGenome()`                  |
| Spawn                       | Vegetative propagation            | Reuse the same individuals        |

`mergeGenome()` treats its two inputs as gametes and builds individuals
whose ploidy is the sum of theirs, so two monokaryons give a dikaryon.
It keeps the haplotypes in order, the first parent's before the
second's, which means the two nuclei of a dikaryon remain identifiable.
`reduceGenome()` halves the ploidy through a full meiosis with
recombination, so a dikaryon gives haploid spores. The crossing
functions `makeCross()`, `randCross()` and `self()` are not used, because
they refuse populations with an odd ploidy.

`AlphaSimR` treats a dikaryon as a diploid individual. The two nuclei of
a real dikaryon stay separate until fruiting, but for genetic values and
meiosis this makes no difference: both nuclei are present in every cell,
and karyogamy takes place immediately before meiosis.

Genetic values remain on one scale across the two stages. Additive
effects are coded so that a haploid carrying an allele receives the same
value as a diploid that is homozygous for it, so a monokaryon's genetic
value equals that of the dikaryon formed by doubling its nucleus. This
allows monokaryons to be given genetic values and phenotypes, although
in practice only dikaryons are evaluated because only they fruit.

`doubleGenome()`, which copies each haplotype in place, models the
special case of a single nucleus duplicating itself. That corresponds to
primary homothallism, in which one nucleus is self-fertile. It is not the
right function for mating between two monokaryons, because the result is
homozygous at every locus and its meiosis produces spores identical to
their parent.

### Mating types

A monokaryon can mate only with a partner of a different mating type.
*P. ostreatus*, like many basidiomycetes, has a tetrapolar mating
system: mating type is determined by two unlinked loci, A and B, each
with many alleles, and two monokaryons form a fertile dikaryon only when
they carry different alleles at both.

`AlphaSimR` has no concept of mating type. Its sexes, set with
`SimParam$setSexes()`, are a two-class system that cannot describe
compatibility at two multiallelic loci. Instead, mating type is treated
here as a property of the genome. Recombination tracking, turned on with
`SimParam$setTrackRec(TRUE)`, records which founder haplotype every
segment of every individual descends from, and `pullIbdHaplo()` reports
it. Each founder nucleus is assumed to carry its own allele at A and at
B, so a monokaryon's mating type is the identity of the founder nucleus
it inherited at the two mating-type loci. The same approach is used for
the sporeless locus below. Compatibility then has to be checked before
every mating, because `mergeGenome()` will combine any two individuals
given to it.

## The breeding program

Oyster mushrooms release enormous numbers of spores, and workers in
oyster mushroom cultivation develop lung problems from breathing them.
A sporeless strain would remove the problem. A naturally sporeless
strain, ATCC 58937, existed, but it was not commercially attractive, so
Wageningen researchers set out to introduce its sporelessness into the
commercial strain HK35 [@baars2005Development]. The resulting variety,
SPOPPO, was released in 2006 [@lavrijssen2020Interruption].

The published description of the program gives its structure
[@baars2005Development; @baars2007Mushroom]:

1.  The two nuclei of each parent strain were recovered as monokaryons
    by protoplasting.
2.  Crosses between the HK35 and ATCC nuclei all produced sporulating
    strains, so sporelessness is recessive: a dikaryon is sporeless
    only when both of its nuclei carry the mutation. Each HK35 nucleus
    was mated with a different ATCC nucleus.
3.  Among the spores of those crosses, the sporeless mutation segregated
    one to one, and genetic markers linked to it were developed.
4.  The mutation was introgressed into each HK35 nucleus separately by
    repeated backcrossing to that nucleus.
5.  The two recombinant nuclei were mated, giving a sporeless strain
    whose genome came mostly from HK35.
6.  Prototype strains were tested on commercial farms.

The later mapping of the trait added one important detail: the sporeless
locus lies on the same linkage group as the A mating-type locus
[@lavrijssen2020Interruption].

That linkage shapes the program. Each backcross mates a selected spore
with the recurrent HK35 nucleus, so the spore must carry mating-type
alleles that differ from that nucleus's at A and at B, which means
carrying the donor's alleles at both. At the end of the program,
however, the two recombinant nuclei must be compatible with each other.
The simplest way to ensure this, and the way that makes the final strain
most like HK35, is for each to carry the mating type of the HK35 nucleus
it replaces. The last spore selected in each line therefore needs the
donor allele at the sporeless locus and the recurrent nucleus's allele
at the A locus on the same chromosome, which requires a crossover
between them.

The published sources do not give the numbers needed for a simulation.
The values below are assumptions, and any of them can be changed.

| Quantity                                   | Value used here         |
|--------------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Chromosomes                                | 11, 1 Morgan each       |
| Sporeless locus                            | Chromosome 3, 30 cM     |
| A mating-type locus                        | Chromosome 3, 55 cM     |
| B mating-type locus                        | Chromosome 7, 50 cM     |
| Spores genotyped per generation            | 200                     |
| Backcross generations                      | 4                       |
| Spores kept per generation                 | 1, then 3 at the end    |
| Yield trial                                | 4 replicates per strain |

*P. ostreatus* has 11 chromosomes, and its genetic map is a little over
1000 cM long [@lavrijssen2020Interruption], so a Morgan per chromosome is
a reasonable approximation. The distance between the sporeless and A
loci is not published and is the assumption that matters most here.

## Setting up the simulation

The founders are simulated with `runMacs()` as haploid genomes. Fifty
are simulated so that the trait has a reference population from which to
set its variance, and four of them serve as the nuclei of the two parent
strains. Yield is modeled as an additive trait. A dominance trait would
be more realistic for dikaryons, but its parameters are defined in the
founder population, and haploid founders have no heterozygotes.

```{r founders}
set.seed(2005)

founderPop = runMacs(nInd = 50, nChr = 11, segSites = 1000, ploidy = 1L)

SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 100, mean = 100, var = 100)
SP$setVarE(varE = 50)
SP$setTrackRec(TRUE)

monokaryons = newPop(founderPop)
monokaryons
```

Each of the three loci is represented by the segregating site closest to
its assumed position.

```{r loci}
genMap = getGenMap()

nearestSite = function(chr, pos){
  onChr = genMap[genMap$chr==chr, ]
  onChr$id[which.min(abs(onChr$pos-pos))]
}

spLocus = nearestSite("3", 0.30)
matA = nearestSite("3", 0.55)
matB = nearestSite("7", 0.50)
```

The parent strains are built by mating their two nuclei. Because the
founders are haploid, each founder contributes exactly one haplotype,
and `pullIbdHaplo()` identifies it by the founder's position in
`founderPop`. The ATCC nuclei, founders 3 and 4, are the ones carrying
the sporeless mutation.

```{r parents}
H = monokaryons[1:2] # HK35 nuclei
S = monokaryons[3:4] # ATCC 58937 nuclei

HK35 = mergeGenome(H, H, crossPlan = cbind(1, 2))
ATCC = mergeGenome(S, S, crossPlan = cbind(1, 2))

c(HK35 = gv(HK35), ATCC = gv(ATCC))
```

## Mating and fruiting

The first step of the program mates an HK35 nucleus with an ATCC
nucleus. The dikaryon fruits and its spores are collected with
`reduceGenome()`. Every spore records the two nuclei it descends from as
its mother and father, which keeps the pedigree correct across the
haploid stage.

```{r firstCross}
F1 = mergeGenome(H[1], S[1], crossPlan = cbind(1, 1))
spores = reduceGenome(F1, nProgeny = 200)

head(data.frame(id = spores@id, mother = spores@mother, father = spores@father))
```

`pullIbdHaplo()` reports, for each spore and each segregating site, the
founder haplotype it inherited. About half the spores carry the
sporeless allele from founder 3, as in the one-to-one segregation that
was observed.

```{r segregation}
ibd = pullIbdHaplo(spores)
table(ibd[, spLocus])
```

The same matrix gives each spore's mating type, and the cross-tabulation
of the two loci on chromosome 3 shows their linkage: spores mostly carry
the sporeless and A-locus alleles of the same founder.

```{r linkage}
table(sporeless = ibd[, spLocus], matingTypeA = ibd[, matA])
```

## Backcrossing into one nucleus

The function below runs the introgression into a single HK35 nucleus. In
each generation it mates the recurrent nucleus with the current
recombinant, collects spores, and keeps the spores that carry the
sporeless allele and a suitable mating type: compatible with the
recurrent nucleus while backcrossing continues, and identical to it in
the last generation. From these it keeps those with the greatest share
of the recurrent nucleus's genome, which is marker-assisted background
selection, or keeps a random set when `useBackground` is `FALSE`.

Here the identity of the founder at each site stands in for genotypes at
markers. A real program genotypes markers linked to the loci, and the
SPOPPO program used markers linked to the sporeless locus.

```{r introgress}
introgress = function(recurrent, donor, nBackcross = 4, nSpores = 200,
                      nFinal = 3, useBackground = TRUE){
  rec = as.integer(recurrent@iid)
  current = donor
  for(gen in 0:nBackcross){
    strain = mergeGenome(recurrent, current, crossPlan = cbind(1, 1))
    spores = reduceGenome(strain, nProgeny = nSpores)
    ibd = pullIbdHaplo(spores)

    sporeless = ibd[, spLocus]!=rec
    if(gen<nBackcross){
      # The spore must still be able to mate with the recurrent nucleus
      mating = ibd[, matA]!=rec & ibd[, matB]!=rec
      n = 1
    }else{
      # The spore must replace the recurrent nucleus in the final strain
      mating = ibd[, matA]==rec & ibd[, matB]==rec
      n = nFinal
    }
    keep = which(sporeless & mating)
    if(length(keep)==0){
      stop("no usable spore in generation ", gen)
    }
    n = min(n, length(keep))

    if(useBackground){
      recovery = rowMeans(ibd[keep, , drop = FALSE]==rec)
      take = keep[order(recovery, decreasing = TRUE)[1:n]]
    }else{
      take = keep[sample.int(length(keep), n)]
    }
    current = spores[take]
  }
  current
}
```

Each HK35 nucleus is paired with a different ATCC nucleus, as in the
program.

```{r lines}
line1 = introgress(recurrent = H[1], donor = S[1])
line2 = introgress(recurrent = H[2], donor = S[2])
```

The plot shows where the final recombinant nuclei of the first line
still carry donor sequence on chromosome 3, with dashed lines at the
sporeless locus and the A mating-type locus. Little donor sequence is
left, and most of what remains is a segment around the sporeless locus,
which selection kept from the donor in every generation. The A locus is
free of it, as the last round of selection required.

```{r drag, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
chr3 = genMap$id[genMap$chr=="3"]
pos3 = genMap$pos[genMap$chr=="3"]
fromDonor = pullIbdHaplo(line1)[, chr3]!=as.integer(H[1]@iid)

plot(range(pos3), c(0.5, nInd(line1)+0.5), type = "n",
     xlab = "Position on chromosome 3 (Morgans)", ylab = "Nucleus",
     yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = 1:nInd(line1))
for(i in 1:nInd(line1)){
  points(pos3[fromDonor[i, ]], rep(i, sum(fromDonor[i, ])),
         pch = 15, cex = 0.5)
}
abline(v = genMap$pos[genMap$id%in%c(spLocus, matA)], lty = 2)
```

## Building and testing prototypes

Every recombinant from the first line carries the mating type of the
first HK35 nucleus and every one from the second carries that of the
second, so any pairing of the two is compatible. Mating them all gives
nine prototype strains, and a strain is sporeless when both of its
nuclei carry the donor allele.

```{r prototypes}
crossPlan = expand.grid(1:nInd(line1), 1:nInd(line2))
prototypes = mergeGenome(line1, line2, crossPlan = as.matrix(crossPlan))

ibd = pullIbdHaplo(prototypes)
isSporeless = ibd[c(TRUE, FALSE), spLocus]%in%S@iid &
  ibd[c(FALSE, TRUE), spLocus]%in%S@iid
all(isSporeless)
```

The prototypes are then tested alongside HK35 in a yield trial with four
replicates.

```{r trial}
trial = c(prototypes, HK35)
trial = setPheno(trial, reps = 4)

data.frame(strain = c(paste0("prototype", 1:nInd(prototypes)), "HK35"),
           gv = round(gv(trial)[, 1], 2), pheno = round(pheno(trial)[, 1], 2))
```

Because the aim of the program is to reproduce HK35, the prototypes'
genetic values should be close to HK35's. Several prototypes have
identical genetic values because their nuclei differ only where no QTL
lie, and the differences among them all are much smaller than the
error in a trial of this size. This matches
what was found for SPOPPO, whose prototypes performed satisfactorily on
farms [@baars2005Development].

## The value of background selection

The simulation can be used to ask how much the marker-assisted
background selection contributes. The loop below repeats the whole
program with new parent strains each time, with and without background
selection, and records the share of the final strain's genome that
comes from HK35 and its genetic value relative to HK35.

```{r replicates}
result = NULL
for(rep in 1:20){
  parents = sample.int(nInd(monokaryons), 4)
  H = monokaryons[parents[1:2]]
  S = monokaryons[parents[3:4]]
  HK35 = mergeGenome(H, H, crossPlan = cbind(1, 2))
  for(useBackground in c(FALSE, TRUE)){
    line1 = introgress(H[1], S[1], nFinal = 1, useBackground = useBackground)
    line2 = introgress(H[2], S[2], nFinal = 1, useBackground = useBackground)
    strain = mergeGenome(line1, line2, crossPlan = cbind(1, 1))
    result = rbind(result, data.frame(
      useBackground = useBackground,
      recovery = mean(pullIbdHaplo(strain)%in%H@iid),
      gvDiff = gv(strain)[, 1]-gv(HK35)[, 1]
    ))
  }
}

aggregate(cbind(recovery, gvDiff) ~ useBackground, data = result,
          FUN = function(x) round(c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)), 3))
```

Without background selection, about 94% of the final strain's genome
comes from HK35 after four backcrosses, and its genetic value differs
from HK35's by an amount that varies widely from one run to the next.
Selecting among the usable spores for the HK35 background raises the
share to about 99% and makes the final strain far more reliably like
HK35. The mean difference is small in both cases because the donor
nuclei were drawn at random, so donor sequence is as likely to help as
to hurt; with a donor known to be poor, the foreground-only program
would also be worse on average.

## What can and cannot be modeled

The program above used only a few features of `AlphaSimR`, but they
cover the sexual cycle of most cultivated basidiomycetes and many
ascomycetes. The list below is a guide to what else can be represented.

**Can be modeled directly**

-   Haploid and diploid stages, using `mergeGenome()` for mating and
    `reduceGenome()` for meiosis. Ploidies other than one and two are
    also supported, as long as meiosis is applied to an even ploidy.
-   Clonal propagation, which needs no function: the same individuals
    are used again.
-   Primary homothallism, with `doubleGenome()` or with
    `mergeGenome()` given the same individual twice.
-   Phenotypes and genetic values in either stage, with a single scale
    for additive effects.
-   Pedigrees through the haploid stage, since spores record their
    parental nuclei.
-   Marker-assisted and genomic selection, using `pullSnpGeno()` or
    `pullIbdHaplo()` on monokaryons or dikaryons.
-   Uneven recombination along chromosomes, with a custom genetic map.
    This is how the button mushroom (*Agaricus bisporus* var.
    *bisporus*), whose crossovers are confined almost entirely to the
    ends of its chromosomes [@sonnenberg2016Detailed], would be
    represented.

**Must be handled by the user**

-   Mating types. `AlphaSimR` will mate any two individuals, so
    compatibility must be checked before each mating, as it was here.
    Mating-type loci with many alleles can be followed with
    `pullIbdHaplo()` as above, or stored with each individual.
-   Recovering the nuclei of a dikaryon, as protoplasting does. There
    is no function for it. Keeping the monokaryons that formed a
    dikaryon is the simplest solution. `reduceGenome()` with
    `simRecomb = FALSE` does not do this, because chromosomes still
    assort independently and its output mixes the two nuclei.

**Cannot be modeled**

-   Tetrads. Each spore from `reduceGenome()` comes from an independent
    meiosis, so the four products of one meiosis, and the mitotic copies
    of them that some ascomycetes package into an ascus, are not
    produced together.
-   Pseudohomothallism, in which a spore receives two compatible
    nuclei, as in most strains of *A. bisporus* var. *bisporus*
    [@sonnenberg2017Developments]. A two-nucleus spore can be imitated
    by mating two spores of the same strain, but `reduceGenome()` does
    not reproduce the way the nuclei are partitioned.
-   Matings between a dikaryon and a monokaryon (the Buller
    phenomenon), in which a nucleus of the dikaryon migrates into the
    monokaryon. The SPOPPO program used this route for some of its
    crosses [@baars2005Development]. Its outcome can be simulated by
    choosing one of the dikaryon's nuclei and mating it with
    `mergeGenome()`.
-   Heterokaryons with more than two nuclear types, the parasexual
    cycle and mitotic recombination.
-   Aneuploidy and chromosome loss.
-   Mitochondrial and other cytoplasmic inheritance.
